q: Under standard precautions, how should a phlebotomist treat a patient's blood and body fluids?
choices: As infectious only if the patient has a known diagnosis
As infectious only if visible blood is present
As potentially infectious regardless of the patient's diagnosis
As infectious only when an isolation sign is posted
why: Standard precautions assume all blood, body fluids, secretions, and non-intact skin are potentially infectious for every patient. Waiting for a known diagnosis or an isolation sign fails, because most infected patients are undiagnosed at the time of the draw.

q: A phlebotomist collects specimens from a patient with confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection. What hand hygiene is required after removing gloves?
choices: Soap and water handwashing, because alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores
Alcohol-based hand rub, because it is faster and equally effective
No hand hygiene, because gloves were worn the entire time
Alcohol rub followed by donning a second pair of gloves
why: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol-based rubs do not kill; the friction of soap-and-water washing physically removes them. The alcohol rub choice is tempting because it is the routine default, but it is specifically inadequate for spore formers.

q: How long should a phlebotomist rub hands together with soap and water during routine handwashing?
choices: At least 5 seconds
At least 10 seconds
At least 60 seconds
At least 20 seconds
why: CDC guidance specifies at least 20 seconds of vigorous scrubbing with soap and water. Ten seconds is a common misremembering and is not long enough to adequately remove transient flora.

q: Which is the correct order for donning personal protective equipment before entering an isolation room?
choices: Gloves, gown, mask, goggles
Gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, gloves
Mask, gloves, gown, goggles
Goggles, gloves, gown, mask
why: Donning goes gown, then mask or respirator, then eye protection, then gloves last so the glove cuffs cover the gown sleeves. Putting gloves on first is wrong because they would then be contaminated while adjusting the other items.

q: Which item is removed FIRST when doffing PPE after a blood draw in a contact precautions room?
choices: Mask or respirator
Goggles
Gloves
Gown
why: Gloves are removed first because they are the most contaminated item; the mask or respirator is removed last, after leaving the room, since it protects the airway until exit. Removing the mask first would expose the face while the hands are still soiled.

q: Immediately after withdrawing the needle from a patient's vein, what should the phlebotomist do with the safety device?
choices: Activate the safety feature before disposing of the needle in the sharps container
Recap the needle using the one-hand scoop technique, then discard it
Set the needle on the tray until the bandage is applied
Remove the needle from the holder and discard the needle alone
why: Engineered sharps injury protection must be activated immediately at the point of use, before disposal. Recapping, even one-handed, is not the standard for a device with a built-in safety feature and adds an unnecessary injury opportunity.

q: A sharps container in a drawing station is three-quarters full. What is the correct action?
choices: Press the contents down to make room
Continue using it until the contents reach the lid
Close and replace it when it reaches the fill line, about two-thirds to three-quarters full
Pour the contents into a red biohazard bag
why: Sharps containers are sealed and replaced at the manufacturer's fill line, typically two-thirds to three-quarters full, to prevent overfilling and protrusion injuries. Never push contents down or transfer them, as both actions put hands near exposed sharps.

q: A phlebotomist sustains a needlestick from a used needle. What is the FIRST action?
choices: Report the injury to the supervisor
Wash the site with soap and running water
Request the source patient's HIV test result
Complete an incident report form
why: The immediate first step is decontaminating the wound by washing with soap and running water; reporting and evaluation follow. Reporting is required but is not first, since delay in cleansing increases inoculum exposure.

q: The OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard is found at which citation?
why: 29 CFR 1910.1030 is the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard. 29 CFR 1910.1200 is the Hazard Communication Standard covering chemicals and SDS, which is a related but different rule.

q: How often must an employer review and update the written exposure control plan?
choices: At least annually and whenever new tasks or procedures affect exposure
Every three years
Only after a documented exposure incident
Only when OSHA conducts an inspection
why: The standard requires review and update at least annually and whenever changes in tasks, procedures, or positions alter occupational exposure. Waiting for an exposure incident or an inspection is reactive and not compliant.

q: Which statement about the hepatitis B vaccination is correct for a newly hired phlebotomist?
choices: The employee must pay a share of the cost
It must be offered at no cost within 10 working days of initial assignment
It is mandatory and cannot be refused
It may be offered only after a documented exposure
why: The employer must offer the vaccine series free of charge within 10 working days of initial assignment to work with exposure risk. The employee may decline, but must sign the OSHA declination form, so calling it mandatory is incorrect.

q: A phlebotomist declines the hepatitis B vaccine. What must happen?
choices: The employee is reassigned to non-exposure duties
The employee forfeits the vaccine permanently
The employee signs a declination form and may still receive the vaccine later at no cost
No documentation is needed if the refusal is verbal
why: A signed OSHA declination form is required, and the employee retains the right to free vaccination at any later date while still covered. Treating the refusal as permanent misstates the standard.

q: Which item belongs in a red biohazard bag rather than regular trash?
choices: A blood-saturated gauze pad
An empty specimen bag with no visible contamination
A paper requisition form
An unused alcohol prep pad wrapper
why: Items saturated or dripping with blood are regulated medical waste and require a biohazard bag. A clean, uncontaminated specimen bag is not regulated waste and overfilling biohazard streams needlessly raises disposal cost.

q: What must appear on a container of regulated medical waste?
choices: The collecting phlebotomist's name and license number
The patient's name and date of birth
The biohazard symbol with fluorescent orange or orange-red background
A green recycling symbol
why: OSHA requires the biohazard legend and symbol on a fluorescent orange or orange-red background, or the use of red bags or containers. Patient identifiers must never appear on waste containers, as that would expose PHI.

q: A tube of blood breaks on the floor. After absorbing the spill and removing glass with forceps, what disinfectant concentration is appropriate?
choices: 1:100 dilution of household bleach
70 percent isopropyl alcohol
Plain soap and water
1:10 dilution of household bleach
why: A 1:10 bleach dilution, roughly 5000 ppm available chlorine, is the standard for blood spill decontamination. A 1:100 dilution is used for routine surface cleaning of non-porous surfaces without gross blood, and alcohol is not appropriate for a blood spill.

q: Where should a phlebotomist look to find the flash point and first aid measures for a chemical used in the lab?
choices: The Safety Data Sheet for that chemical
The laboratory procedure manual
The exposure control plan
The Joint Commission standards manual
why: Safety Data Sheets contain a standardized 16 sections covering hazards, handling, first aid, and physical properties such as flash point. The exposure control plan addresses bloodborne pathogens, not chemical properties.

q: On an NFPA 704 diamond, what does the blue quadrant indicate?
choices: Flammability
Health hazard
Reactivity or instability
Special hazards such as oxidizer
why: Blue is health, red is flammability, yellow is reactivity, and white is special hazards. Red and blue are frequently swapped by test takers, so anchor on blue equals health.

q: What does the acronym RACE stand for in hospital fire response?
choices: Report, Alert, Contain, Escape
Remove, Alarm, Contain or Confine, Extinguish or Evacuate
Respond, Assess, Call, Evacuate
Rescue, Assess, Close, Exit
why: RACE is Rescue or Remove people in danger, Alarm, Contain or Confine the fire by closing doors, then Extinguish or Evacuate. Rescuing people always precedes attempting to extinguish, which is why options that lead with assessing or calling are wrong.

q: A small electrical fire starts in a centrifuge. Which extinguisher class is appropriate?
choices: Class A
Class B
Class D
Class C
why: Class C extinguishers are rated for energized electrical equipment. Class A is for ordinary combustibles such as paper and would use water, which conducts electricity and creates a shock hazard.

q: Using the PASS technique, what does the second S represent?
choices: Sweep the nozzle side to side at the base of the fire
Shut the door behind you
Stand six feet back
Signal for assistance
why: PASS is Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side. Aiming at the flames rather than the base, or confusing the step with signaling, will fail to smother the fuel source.

q: A phlebotomist notices a frayed cord on a blood collection cart's power strip. What is the correct action?
choices: Wrap the cord in electrical tape and continue using it
Remove the equipment from service, tag it, and report it to maintenance
Use it only for low-draw devices
Unplug it at the end of the shift and report it next week
why: Damaged electrical equipment must be taken out of service and reported immediately, because a frayed cord is both a shock and a fire hazard. Field repairs with tape are not acceptable and leave the hazard in place.

q: A phlebotomist must draw a patient in the radiology suite during an active imaging procedure. Which principle minimizes radiation exposure?
choices: Wear a surgical mask and double gloves
Face the radiation source at all times
Maximize distance, minimize time, and use shielding
Stand directly behind the imaging tube
why: Time, distance, and shielding are the three cardinal principles of radiation protection. PPE for infection control offers no protection from ionizing radiation, which is why the mask and gloves option is a distractor.

q: A patient is on airborne precautions for suspected tuberculosis. What respiratory protection does the phlebotomist need?
choices: A fit-tested N95 respirator or higher
A standard surgical mask
A face shield alone
No respiratory protection if the draw takes under five minutes
why: Airborne precautions require a fit-tested N95 or higher-level respirator because droplet nuclei stay suspended and travel on air currents. A surgical mask is adequate for droplet precautions such as influenza, but does not seal or filter to the N95 level.

q: Which precaution category is correct for a patient with suspected pertussis?
choices: Airborne precautions with a negative-pressure room
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask within three to six feet
Contact precautions only
Standard precautions only
why: Pertussis spreads by large respiratory droplets that travel only about three to six feet, so droplet precautions with a surgical mask apply. Airborne precautions and negative pressure are reserved for tuberculosis, measles, and varicella.

q: In the chain of infection, a contaminated tourniquet reused between patients best represents which link?
choices: Reservoir
Portal of entry
Mode of transmission
Susceptible host
why: The tourniquet acts as a vehicle carrying organisms from one person to another, which is the mode of transmission link. The reservoir is where the pathogen normally lives and multiplies, not the object that merely carries it.

q: Which practice reflects correct body mechanics when a phlebotomist lifts a heavy box of supplies?
choices: Bend at the waist and lift with the back
Twist at the waist while lifting to save a step
Hold the load away from the body for better visibility
Bend the knees, keep the back straight, and hold the load close to the body
why: Squatting with a straight back and keeping the load close uses the strong leg muscles and reduces lumbar strain. Twisting while loaded is a common cause of back injury and should be replaced by pivoting with the feet.

q: A patient reports a latex allergy before a venipuncture. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Use nitrile gloves and a latex-free tourniquet and bandage
Use latex gloves but wash hands first
Use powdered latex gloves to reduce contact
Proceed normally, since a brief contact is harmless
why: All latex-containing items in the encounter, including the tourniquet and bandage, must be replaced with latex-free alternatives. Powdered latex gloves are actually worse, because the powder aerosolizes latex protein.

q: Which organization or regulation governs all laboratory testing performed on human specimens in the United States for the purpose of diagnosis?
choices: The Joint Commission
CLSI
CLIA
CDC
why: CLIA is the federal regulation establishing quality standards for all non-research human laboratory testing. CLSI writes consensus standards and guidelines such as GP41 for venipuncture, but those are voluntary rather than regulatory.

q: Running a normal and abnormal control on a glucose meter before testing patient samples is an example of what?
choices: Quality assurance
Quality control
Proficiency testing
A delta check
why: Quality control is the measurable testing of known materials to verify the analytic system is working. Quality assurance is the broader program covering the whole pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic process, of which QC is one component.

q: A phlebotomist mislabels a tube and the error is caught before testing. What should happen?
choices: Correct the label quietly and say nothing, since no harm occurred
Document the event on an incident or occurrence report and notify the supervisor
Note the error only in the patient's chart
Discard the tube and take no further action
why: Near misses are reported on an incident report so trends can be tracked and processes improved. Silently correcting the label hides data from the quality assurance program, even though the patient was not harmed.

q: A coworker asks about a celebrity patient whose blood the phlebotomist just drew. Under HIPAA, what is the correct response?
choices: Share the information because the coworker is also an employee
Share only the diagnosis, not the name
Share the information if the coworker promises confidentiality
Decline, because the coworker has no treatment-related need to know
why: HIPAA allows disclosure only to those with a legitimate treatment, payment, or operations need, under the minimum necessary standard. Being an employee does not by itself create a need to know.

q: Which action best demonstrates the HIPAA minimum necessary standard?
choices: Accessing only the requisition information required to perform the assigned draw
Reviewing the full chart to better understand the patient
Printing the complete medical record to carry on rounds
Discussing the case in the elevator with another technician
why: Minimum necessary limits access and disclosure to the smallest amount of PHI needed for the task. Reading the full chart out of curiosity exceeds what the draw requires, even when the intent is benign.

q: A competent adult inpatient says no when the phlebotomist approaches to draw blood. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Proceed, because the physician ordered the test
Ask a nurse to hold the patient's arm
Stop, document the refusal, and notify the nurse or provider
Wait ten minutes and attempt the draw while the patient sleeps
why: A competent patient has the right to refuse, and proceeding over that refusal could constitute battery. A physician order authorizes the test but does not override the patient's consent.

q: A phlebotomist raises a needle toward a patient who has said no and the patient reasonably fears being stuck. Which term describes this act?
choices: Negligence
Assault
Battery
Res ipsa loquitur
why: Assault is the threat or apprehension of harmful contact; battery is the actual unconsented touching. The distinction matters because the needle has not yet touched the patient in this scenario.

q: A patient asks the phlebotomist what an elevated potassium result means for her health. What is the appropriate response within scope of practice?
choices: Explain the general clinical significance of high potassium
Tell the patient the result is probably nothing to worry about
Refer the patient to her provider, who will interpret and discuss the results
Look up the reference range and read it aloud to reassure her
why: Interpreting laboratory results is outside a phlebotomist's scope of practice and belongs to the ordering provider. Offering reassurance that the value is harmless is equally out of scope and could delay needed care.
